articles.title: A Checkerboard Is Not Transparency: A Practical Alpha Test for Video
articles.excerpt: You export a “background-free” video, put it on a web page, and see a black rectangle. Is the file broken? Perhaps. But the player might be ignoring a real alpha channel. Before running background rem…
articles.body: You export a “background-free” video, put it on a web page, and see a black rectangle. Is the file broken? Perhaps. But the player might be ignoring a real alpha channel. Before running background removal again, separate three things: the preview background , the file's alpha channel , and the software playing the file . They can produce similar-looking screenshots for very different reasons. Start with a no-code test Place the exported file above a bright, solid-color layer in a video editor that supports transparency. Change that layer to a very different color. Watch the space around the subject, then pause on frames with hair, hands, or motion blur. If both colors show through around the subject, the file is being composited with transparency in that editor.
articles.author: river

articles.title: People Are Already Using Obsidian as Their Agent's Memory. Here's the Production Version.
articles.excerpt: A post this week walks through using Obsidian plus Claude Code as a shared memory stack the author actually runs. Not a thought experiment. Developers are already treating their local notes as the lay…
articles.body: A post this week walks through using Obsidian plus Claude Code as a shared memory stack the author actually runs. Not a thought experiment. Developers are already treating their local notes as the layer their agent reads and writes across sessions. Two more posts from the same week sit on either side of it. One argues that agents do not need memory at all, they need documentation. A Show HN pitches a memory layer that makes coding agents cheaper on repeat work. Everyone agrees the notes-plus-context story is broken. Nobody agrees on what replaces it. The instinct in the Obsidian post is right, and the missing piece is easy to state and hard to build: a notes folder is not yet a memory system.

articles.title: Same proxy IP, lost login: which session expired?
articles.excerpt: A browser automation job can keep the same proxy exit IP and still lose its login. Before changing the proxy settings, separate two kinds of state: the exit assignment managed by the proxy service and…
articles.body: A browser automation job can keep the same proxy exit IP and still lose its login. Before changing the proxy settings, separate two kinds of state: the exit assignment managed by the proxy service and the website session maintained by your client. Two sessions with different jobs A sticky proxy session asks the provider to keep an exit assignment for a task. A common implementation uses a session label in the proxy settings, although some services use a sticky port or a dashboard option. Use the format documented for that product; adding a parameter to the destination website URL does not configure the proxy. The website session usually depends on cookies or authentication tokens. Keeping an IP does not store those values, send them on subsequent requests, or extend the website login.

articles.title: A prototype AI agent can survive on a static CSV and a single Python script. A production agent cannot.
articles.excerpt: I recently completed the AI-Assisted Data Science with BigQuery lab via Google Cloud. While analyzing the final multimodal vector search stage, I focused heavily on how the pipeline enforces state dep…
articles.body: I recently completed the AI-Assisted Data Science with BigQuery lab via Google Cloud. While analyzing the final multimodal vector search stage, I focused heavily on how the pipeline enforces state dependencies. If the remote multimodal_embedding_model isn't strictly instantiated within the dataset first, the system throws a hard blocker. In an isolated sandbox, that’s just a minor execution step. But in a production multi-agent system? That is a catastrophic DAG dependency failure. This constraint perfectly exposes the exact bottleneck the AI industry is hitting today. We spend all our time building the orchestration loops, and almost zero time engineering the rigid data pipelines required to feed them.

articles.title: Solo-Founders Struggle: How Lack of Team Support Limits Startup Scalability
articles.excerpt: The "solopreneur model is hitting a hard operational ceiling. For the past few years, modern business culture has heavily promoted the concept of the absolute independent operator, the single founder…
articles.body: The "solopreneur model is hitting a hard operational ceiling. For the past few years, modern business culture has heavily promoted the concept of the absolute independent operator, the single founder using automated software and digital tools to run a lean, highly profitable enterprise without building an actual organization. It sounds like the ultimate lean setup. However, once a business moves past the initial launch phase, it runs into an unyielding economic law: you cannot build a truly scalable enterprise in total isolation. The ongoing Solo-Founders Struggle is a direct look at how a missing human infrastructure slows down development, caps revenue potential, and leaves early-stage startups and MSMEs vulnerable to market shifts.

articles.title: Are We Building AI Agents We Can No Longer Control?
articles.excerpt: AI agents are moving beyond generating code. They can now execute commands, modify files, browse the web, and coordinate with other agents. But here's the question: How much autonomy should we give an…
articles.body: AI agents are moving beyond generating code. They can now execute commands, modify files, browse the web, and coordinate with other agents. But here's the question: How much autonomy should we give an AI agent before the security risks outweigh the productivity gains? Should agents require human approval for every sensitive action, or should we trust them to operate independently within predefined boundaries? I'm curious how other developers are approaching this in real-world projects. Where do you draw the line between useful autonomy and dangerous overreach?

articles.title: Lookout: The Offline AI Field Companion That Tells You to Put Your Phone Away
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass I built Lookout, a privacy-first Android field companion designed around one unusual success metric: The AI shou…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built I built Lookout , a privacy-first Android field companion designed around one unusual success metric: The AI should help you stop using the AI. Most outdoor apps pull people deeper into their screens: more photos, more feeds, more badges, more notifications. Lookout takes the opposite approach. You ask a question about what you notice outdoors, receive one useful fact and a small observation mission, then the app encourages you to put the phone away and pay attention to the world around you. It is for walkers, beginner birders, students, hikers, and anyone who wants technology to support outdoor curiosity without becoming another distraction.

articles.body: Full spoilers follow for War: Season 1 , Episode 2. After a heavy dose of frenetic table-setting in the series premiere , War’s second episode — sharply written by George Kay and deftly directed by Ben Taylor — slows its pacing down a bit as Morgan (Dominic West) and Carla (Sienna Miller) and their respective legal teams enter the pivotal three-day mediation period of their divorce. Morgan and Carla are each instructed by their teams to put on amicable fronts as both sides strategize how to strike the best deal. That means a lot of strained smiles and literal hand-holding between the divorcing spouses to mask any anger and bitterness. Their facades just barely hold. Behind the scenes, their teams are reckoning how to protect their clients and gain the upper hand.
